AQ Biotech services

Biomarker Discovery as a Service

AQ Enigma is AQ Biotech’s platform for delivering biomarker discovery services and conducting research. We use phage biosensor signals to compare samples, with a focus on oncology, neurodegenerative disease and infectious disease.

Phage biosensors for disease research

Phage biosensors convert interactions with molecules in a sample into measurable signals. AQ Biotech studies these signals to look for patterns that may be associated with disease.

Our projects

Explore the research underway across our pipeline.

Advantages of phage biosensors

Non-invasive sampling

Urine and saliva can be collected without an invasive procedure. Sample choice depends on the study.

Multi-omics

Sensor readings can be studied alongside other molecular measurements.

Specificity

Researchers can study which targets or sample conditions produce different sensor responses.

Scalability

Instrument-based readouts offer a consistent format for comparing signals across samples.

Kidney diseases

The Nanjing project studies biosensor signals associated with kidney disease. Sample collection is underway.

Study focus
The study explores whether patterns across biosensor readings can help identify candidate signals for kidney disease research.
Research collaborators
The project involves Jiangsu Public Hospital and KingMed Diagnostics.

Parkinson’s disease

Phage biosensors developed in Turku, Finland, were selected for testing in a larger, independent cohort in Chengdu, China.

Study question
The study asks whether biosensor signals in urine and serum differ between Parkinson’s disease, other neurological conditions and healthy controls.

Turku, Finland

Finnish cohort

The study compared samples from different stages of Parkinson’s disease with samples from other neurological conditions and healthy controls. Candidate sensors were selected for further testing.

Chengdu, China

Chinese cohort

The Chinese cohort adds conditions that can be difficult to distinguish from Parkinson’s disease, such as multiple system atrophy. Testing covers both urine and serum, and new sensors are developed for each sample type.

Lung cancer

The lung cancer project investigates biosensor signals associated with lung cancer. The research involves teams in Shanghai and Chengdu.

Research teams
The project involves the Shanghai Institute of Infectious Diseases and West China Hospital.
Planned milestones
The research and assay validation report is planned for December 2026. The clinical validation phase is scheduled to start in January 2027.

Prostate cancer

The research develops urine-based biosensors for prostate cancer detection. Biosensor signals were studied in Finland using samples from Helsinki University Hospital. Selected biosensor candidates were taken forward to pre-clinical validation in a Chinese cohort at Jiangsu Cancer Hospital in Nanjing.

Research milestone
The team reported on the project in September 2026.
Next step
AQ is seeking a partner for the next stage of the project.

Metastatic cancers

The research focuses on detecting different metastatic cancers from urine samples. The sample collection and research is being conducted in Turku and Nanjing.

Research teams
Turku University Hospital and Jiangsu Cancer Hospital participate in the study.
Research focus
The study looks for patterns across sensor readings that may be associated with metastatic cancer.

Organ transplantation

The current research focuses on studying phage biosensor signals associated with chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD) and non-CLAD after lung transplantation, using urine, saliva and plasma samples.

Study question
The study asks whether biosensor readings can reveal patterns associated with rejection in lung transplant recipients.
Research status
The study with Baylor St. Luke’s Medical Center is ongoing.

Tuberculosis

The project studies biosensor signals associated with tuberculosis in collaboration with the Shanghai Public Health Clinical Center.

Study focus
The study explores whether biosensor readings can reveal patterns associated with tuberculosis.
Planned milestones
The research and assay validation report is planned for December 2026. The clinical validation phase is scheduled to start in January 2027.

Sepsis

The sepsis project studies disease-associated biosensor signals at Max Nanavati Hospital in Mumbai.

Study focus
The study explores patterns across biosensor readings that may be associated with sepsis.
Project stage
The project is in the research and assay validation phase, with a milestone scheduled for December 2026.

AQ Enigma technology

Can a protein have a fingerprint?

Some sensors may respond more strongly to a protein than others. Put the readings in order and the pattern becomes a fingerprint.

Why look at a group of readings?

A single reading tells you how one sensor responded. Together, the readings show which signals shift as the protein changes state and which stay steady.

AQ Enigma studies protein responses using biosensors developed from bacteriophages.

Biomarker discovery

Biomarker discovery with phage biosensors

A biomarker is a measurable indicator of a biological state. Discovery starts by finding candidates and asking whether they are linked to the change you care about.

Researchers use phage biosensors to look for signals linked to a disease or biological state. AQ Enigma brings together readings from selected protein biosensors to compare proteins and examine how their signals change across states.

AQ Enigma research

Research evidence

Explore the protein-state experiments, sensor library, and comparison with predicted protein structures.

Transferrin experiment

How does the signal differ with and without iron?

Transferrin carries iron in the blood. This experiment compares its sensor readings in the iron-bound and iron-free states.

  • Solid orange: iron-free
  • Solid blue: iron-bound

At all three time points shown in this experiment, the iron-free form gave higher readings. This gives researchers a concrete example of comparing two states of the same protein. The dashed lines show the comparison after heat denaturation.

How does glucose binding change the signal?

Concanavalin A is a protein that binds sugars. A glucose experiment compared two states. The chart shows a lower signal when the binding site was occupied than when it was free, giving the team another example of how binding can affect the readout.

Sensor library

How a panel forms a fingerprint

The same protein can give different readings across sensors. A panel lets researchers ask whether similarly shaped proteins leave similar patterns.

Five protein structure groups of interest

  • Mostly alpha-helical globular proteins
  • Mostly beta-sheet globular proteins
  • Globular proteins with both alpha helices and beta sheets
  • Fibrous or rod-like proteins
  • Multidomain signaling proteins

Alpha helices and beta sheets are two common ways a protein chain folds.

Structural comparison

How do the signals compare with AlphaFold predictions?

Researchers used AlphaFold’s predicted structures to ask whether sensor signals vary with the distance between parts of a protein.

The horizontal axis shows the predicted distance between domains. The vertical axis shows the relative sensor response. Both trend lines rise in this set of proteins, so larger predicted distances tended to go with higher readings.

A next research question is whether this relationship holds across more proteins.

Research progress since July 2026

Experimental findings

Protein fingerprinting
Proof-of-principle experiments showed different sensor readings for different states of the same protein.
Protein surface features
The team is studying what biosensor responses can reveal about protein surfaces alongside AlphaFold predictions.
Structural comparison
The team reports reproducing correlations between biosensor readings and AlphaFold predictions. Higher-resolution analysis is underway.

Ongoing research

Patient sample pilot
Pilot testing uses patient samples to explore whether sensor readings can characterize protein profiles.
Functional assays
The team is assessing AQ Enigma in functional assays using medically relevant targets and receptor-binding models.

Discuss a research collaboration

  • Compare two states of one protein For example, does the sensor pattern differ with and without a bound molecule?
  • Compare structurally similar proteins For example, do two similarly shaped proteins produce similar signals?
